sec.t:
आम [[@waves-how|लहरें]] हवा से बनती हैं। वे समुद्र के बस ऊपरी कुछ मीटर पानी को हिलाती हैं, और एक लहर की चोटी से अगली चोटी तक की दूरी कुछ मीटर या दसियों मीटर होती है।

सुनामी अलग है। जब समुद्र का तल उछलता है, तो वह अपने ऊपर के पूरे पानी को धकेल देता है, तली से लेकर सतह तक, जो कई किलोमीटर गहरा हो सकता है। जो लहर फैलती है, उसकी एक चोटी से दूसरी चोटी तक की दूरी सैकड़ों किलोमीटर हो सकती है। इसीलिए उसमें इतनी ज़्यादा [[energy|ऊर्जा]] होती है, और इसीलिए वह किनारे की आम लहर की तरह टूटकर ख़त्म नहीं हो जाती।

"सुनामी" जापानी भाषा का शब्द है, जिसका मतलब है "बंदरगाह की लहर"। यह [[@tides|ज्वार-भाटे]] से नहीं आती, हालाँकि लोग कभी-कभी इसे ज्वारीय लहर कह देते हैं। बड़े [[@landslides|भूस्खलन]], ज्वालामुखी विस्फोट और बहुत ही कम मामलों में [[asteroid|क्षुद्रग्रहों]] की टक्कर से भी सुनामी उठ सकती है।

गहरे समुद्र में सुनामी लगभग 800 किमी प्रति घंटा तक की रफ़्तार से चल सकती है, यानी किसी यात्री जेट जितनी तेज़। बंगाल की खाड़ी को वह कोई दो घंटे में पार कर सकती है। जब वह तट के पास उथले पानी में पहुँचती है, तो उसका अगला हिस्सा धीमा पड़ जाता है, जबकि पीछे का पानी आता ही रहता है। लहर ऊँची, और ऊँची होती जाती है।

कभी-कभी लोगों को सबसे पहले कोई लहर दिखती ही नहीं। समुद्र अचानक पीछे हट जाता है और रेत पर मछलियाँ तड़पती छूट जाती हैं। यह फ़ौरन ज़मीन की तरफ़ और ऊँचाई पर भागने की चेतावनी है। 2011 में जापान में आई सुनामी कुछ जगहों पर लगभग 40 मीटर ऊँची थी। यह किसी 13 मंज़िला इमारत जितनी ऊँचाई है।

अब तक की सबसे ऊँची दर्ज लहर 1958 में [[@alaska|अलास्का]] की लिटुया खाड़ी में उठी थी। एक भूकंप ने चट्टानों का एक विशाल ढेर एक तंग खाड़ी में गिरा दिया। उससे उछले पानी ने सामने की पहाड़ी पर 500 मीटर से भी ज़्यादा ऊँचाई तक के पेड़ उखाड़ डाले।

{{story:waves-how}}

26 दिसंबर 2004 को इंडोनेशिया के सुमात्रा के पास समुद्र के नीचे 9.1 तीव्रता का भूकंप आया। सुनामी की लहरें पूरे हिंद महासागर में फैल गईं और [[@thailand|थाईलैंड]], [[@sri-lanka|श्रीलंका]], भारत, [[@maldives|मालदीव]] और पूर्वी अफ़्रीका तक पहुँचीं। यह आधुनिक इतिहास की सबसे जानलेवा प्राकृतिक आपदाओं में से एक थी।

भारत में तमिलनाडु के तट, ख़ासकर नागपट्टिनम के आसपास, और [[@andaman|अंडमान और निकोबार द्वीप समूह]] सबसे ज़्यादा प्रभावित हुए। भूकंप के बेहद पास बसे इंडोनेशिया के सिमयुलुए द्वीप पर लोगों को एक पुरानी स्थानीय कहानी सिखाती थी कि समुद्र पीछे हटे तो पहाड़ियों की ओर भागो। वे इसे "स्मोंग" कहते थे। लोगों को यह बात याद थी, इसलिए द्वीप के ज़्यादातर निवासी बच गए।

उस समय हिंद महासागर के लिए कोई सुनामी चेतावनी प्रणाली नहीं थी। 2007 से हैदराबाद में INCOIS का भारतीय सुनामी पूर्व चेतावनी केंद्र चौबीसों घंटे समुद्र के नीचे के भूकंपों पर नज़र रखता है। इसके लिए वह भूकंप नापने वाले यंत्रों, ज्वार नापने वाले यंत्रों और गहरे समुद्र के तल पर लगे दबाव [[sensor|सेंसरों]] का इस्तेमाल करता है। ये सेंसर अपने ऊपर से गुज़रती सुनामी को महसूस कर सकते हैं।

प्रशांत महासागर में 1949 से [[@hawaii-islands|हवाई]] में एक चेतावनी केंद्र है। समुद्र के नीचे कोई बड़ा भूकंप पकड़ में आते ही कुछ ही मिनटों में तटों तक चेतावनी पहुँच सकती है।

text: Auroras happen when [[@solar-wind|particles from the Sun]] hit our air and make it glow.
Earth's magnetic field guides them towards the poles, so auroras are usually seen near the Arctic and Antarctica.
During a huge solar storm in May 2024, an aurora was photographed from Hanle in Ladakh!

The glowing gases are the same ones you breathe. Oxygen makes most of the green and red, and nitrogen adds blue and purple. Together they form rippling curtains, arcs and rays that can stretch across the whole sky.

sec.t:
The Sun constantly blows out a thin stream of electrically charged particles, mostly [[proton|protons]] and [[electron|electrons]]. This is called the solar wind. It rushes through space at around 400 km every second, fast enough to cross from Kanyakumari to Kashmir in about 10 seconds.

Sometimes [[@sun-what|the Sun]] hurls out a much bigger cloud of charged gas, called a coronal mass ejection. If one is aimed at Earth, it arrives about one to three days later. India's [[@aditya-l1|Aditya-L1]] spacecraft watches the Sun from 1.5 million km away and helps scientists see such storms coming.

Deep [[@inside-earth|inside Earth]], molten iron swirling in the outer core creates a [[@earth-magnet|magnetic field]] that stretches far out into space. It acts like a shield, steering most of the solar wind around our planet.

{{story:earth-magnet}}

But the field lines curve down into Earth near the North and South Poles. Some particles get trapped and are funnelled down along these lines. About 100 to 300 km above the ground, they crash into [[atom|atoms]] of oxygen and nitrogen and give them extra energy. The atoms quickly get rid of it as flashes of light. Billions of these flashes together make an aurora.

The result is usually an oval ring of light around each magnetic pole. Places under the ring, like northern Norway, Iceland, Alaska and northern Canada, see auroras on many clear, dark nights.

The most common colour is a pale green, made by oxygen around 100 to 250 km up. Above that, where the air is extremely thin, oxygen glows a deep red. Nitrogen, lower down, adds blue and purple fringes. Aurora photos often look brighter than the real thing, because cameras collect light longer than our eyes do.

The northern lights are called the aurora borealis, after Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn, and Boreas, the Greek name for the north wind. The southern lights are the aurora australis. Auroras in the north and south often happen at the same time, almost mirror images of each other.

When a really powerful solar storm hits, the oval of light spreads far from the poles. On 10 and 11 May 2024, during the strongest geomagnetic storm in more than 20 years, auroras were seen as far south as Mexico and Florida.

In India, cameras at the Indian Astronomical Observatory at Hanle, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], recorded a reddish glow on the northern horizon. Ladakh is high, dry and dark, so faint light is easier to catch there. Seeing an aurora from India is very rare.

Storms like these can also disturb radio signals, upset GPS and damage satellites, so [[@space-weather|space weather]] forecasters keep a close eye on the Sun.

Earth isn't the only planet with auroras. The [[@hubble|Hubble Space Telescope]] has photographed glowing rings around the poles of [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]] and Saturn. Jupiter's auroras are hundreds of times more powerful than Earth's, fed partly by material from its [[@space-weird-volcano-moon|volcanic moon Io]].

Like [[@lightning|lightning]], an aurora is electricity lighting up the air, but on a scale large enough to be [[@earth-from-space|seen from space]]. Astronauts on the [[@space-station|space station]] sometimes look down on green curtains of light flowing beneath them.

text: Space is so big that the numbers stop making sense. The Moon is about 384,400 kilometres away. The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away, nearly 400 times farther. And the nearest other star is about 40 trillion kilometres away.

To cope, [[astronomer|astronomers]] measure using light. Light is the fastest thing there is, about 300,000 kilometres every second. It crosses from the Moon to Earth in just over one second, but takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to arrive from the Sun. Light from the nearest star takes more than four years, so we say it is about 4.2 [[@light-years|light-years]] away.

sec.t:
Another trick is to make a [[@maps-scale|scale]] model, like a map. Shrink the Sun to the size of a football, about 22 centimetres across. At that scale, Earth is a peppercorn about 24 metres away, the length of a cricket pitch plus a bit. The Moon is a speck of dust about 6 centimetres from the peppercorn.

Jupiter would be a small marble about 120 metres away, and Neptune would be a grain of rice about 700 metres away. Then comes the shock. The nearest star would be another football more than 6,000 kilometres away, about as far as Delhi is from London. Everything in between is almost empty.

Kilometres soon get clumsy, so astronomers use bigger rulers. Inside the [[solar-system|solar system]], they use the astronomical unit, or AU, which is the average distance from Earth to the Sun: about 150 million kilometres. Jupiter is about 5 AU from the Sun, and Neptune about 30.

For stars, they use the [[lightyear|light-year]], the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Professional astronomers often use another unit called the parsec, which is about 3.26 light-years. Using these rulers is a bit like measuring a road trip in hours rather than centimetres. The numbers become small enough to compare in your head.

In 1977, NASA launched two spacecraft called Voyager. [[@voyager|Voyager 1]] has been flying away from us ever since, at about 17 kilometres every second. That is fast enough to cross India from Kashmir to Kanyakumari in under four minutes.

In mid-November 2026, Voyager 1 reaches about one light-day from Earth, roughly 25.9 billion kilometres away. A radio command sent from NASA then takes about 24 hours to reach it, and the reply takes another 24 hours to come back. Even at its speed, Voyager would need more than 70,000 years to travel as far as the nearest star.

Because light takes time to travel, looking into space means looking into the past. You see the Moon as it was a little over a second ago, and the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.

On a dark night, you can spot the Andromeda Galaxy as a faint smudge. It is about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light reaching your eyes left it before modern humans existed. Our own [[@milky-way|Milky Way]] is about 100,000 light-years across, and it is only one of billions of [[@galaxies|galaxies]]. Astronomers have seen light that has been travelling for more than 13 billion years.

text: Birds build nests with their beaks, feet and bodies, one piece at a time. A bird may fly back and forth hundreds of times, carrying twigs, grass, mud, moss, feathers or spider silk.

Each kind of bird has its own style. Some pile up sticks. Some weave, some sew, and some plaster with mud. Most birds shape the cup by sitting in it and turning round and round, pressing the sides out with their chest. The finished nest keeps eggs and chicks warm, hidden and safe from falling.

sec.t:
India's baya weaver builds one of the cleverest nests of all. During the [[monsoon|monsoon]], the male tears long strips from grass or palm leaves and knots them around a branch, often hanging over water. Then he weaves the strips in and out to make a ball with a long entrance tube pointing down. Snakes and crows find it hard to get in.

The male builds a half-finished nest first, then hangs from it, flapping and calling to females. A female inspects it, tugging at the strips. If she likes it, the male finishes the job. If not, he may start again. Studies of weaverbirds in Africa found that males get neater and faster with practice, so building is partly a skill they learn.

sec.h: Spit, silk and stacks of sticks
sec.t:
Some [[@swifts-swallows|swiftlets]] in Southeast Asia, and on India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands, build small cup nests almost entirely from their own [[@gross-saliva|saliva]], which hardens like glue. People collect these nests to make bird's nest soup, which has put some colonies in danger.

[[@hummingbirds|Hummingbirds]] use stretchy [[@spiders-silk|spider silk]] to bind their nests together, so the nest can stretch as the chicks grow. Eagles go the other way. They add sticks to the same nest year after year. A [[@bald-eagle|bald eagle]] nest near St. Petersburg, Florida, measured about 2.9 m wide and 6 m deep, and was thought to weigh around 2 tonnes, about as much as a car.

Not every bird bothers. Many seabirds and lapwings lay eggs straight on bare ground, where their [[@camouflage|speckled colours hide them]]. [[@penguins-cold|Emperor penguins]] balance their egg on their feet.

Some birds borrow other nests. In India, the koel, famous for its loud call in summer, lays its eggs in crows' nests and lets the crows raise its chicks. Hornbills use tree holes. The female [[@hornbills|great hornbill]] seals herself inside with mud and droppings, leaving only a narrow slit. The male feeds her through the slit for weeks while she sits on the eggs.

Nests have inspired human builders, from woven baskets to the "Bird's Nest" stadium built for the 2008 [[@olympics-host|Beijing Olympics]]. Weavers knot grass much as people knot thread on a loom, as you can see in [[@weaving-saree|how a saree is woven]]. But a bird has no hands, no plan on paper and no teacher, just a beak, practice and instinct.

text: The deep sea is cold, dark and under enormous [[pressure|pressure]]. Sunlight fades away within the first few hundred metres, so below about 1,000 metres it is pitch black forever. The water is close to freezing. Food is scarce, because nothing grows without light.

Yet the deep is full of life, and the animals there have found clever ways to cope. Their bodies are soft and watery, so pressure doesn't crush them. Many make their own light. They save energy by moving slowly, and they eat whatever falls from above, or get food from [[bacteria|bacteria]] that live on chemicals instead of sunlight.

st.prompt: Why aren't deep-sea animals crushed flat by the huge pressure?

options.t: Their bodies are mostly water, which hardly squeezes, and they have no air pockets
They have super-thick shells like tanks
The pressure is lower near the sea floor

st.reveal: Water barely shrinks when you squeeze it, so a body full of water pushes back as hard as the sea pushes in. The danger is air spaces, which do get crushed. Deep-sea fish have no air-filled swim bladders, and their proteins are built to keep working under pressure.

src: NOAA Ocean Exploration, deep-sea life and the hadal zone.
University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology, deepest fish footage (2023 announcement).

Explorers have found life even in Challenger Deep, nearly 11 km down. Tiny shrimp-like amphipods, sea cucumbers, single-celled creatures and many kinds of microbe live there, feeding on scraps that drift down from above.

sec.t:
Every 10 metres you go down, the weight of water above adds about one more "[[atmosphere|atmosphere]]" of pressure. At the bottom of Challenger Deep, in the [[@ocean-deepest|Mariana Trench]], it is more than 1,000 atmospheres. That's like having a small car resting on each square centimetre of your skin.

Humans can only go there inside thick metal spheres. A fish is a different story. Its body is mostly water, which hardly squeezes, so the pressure inside it matches the pressure outside. Deep-sea fish also make a special chemical called TMAO that helps their [[protein|proteins]] keep their shape. Some scientists think fish can't live much below about 8,200 to 8,400 metres, because they can't pack in enough of this chemical.

Most deep animals live on "marine snow", a steady drizzle of dead [[plankton|plankton]], droppings and other scraps sinking from the sunlit waters. It can take weeks to reach the bottom. Animals there have huge mouths, stretchy stomachs and slow lives, so they can survive on rare meals.

When a whale dies and sinks, it becomes a feast called a whale fall. Hagfish, crabs, worms and bacteria can feed on a single whale skeleton for decades.

In a few places, there is another food source. Around hot springs on the sea floor, called [[@deep-sea-vents|vents]], bacteria use chemicals from the Earth to make food without sunlight. Tubeworms, crabs and shrimp crowd around them, as busy as any coral reef.

{{story:first-life}}

In the deep, many animals glow. This light, called [[bioluminescence|bioluminescence]], is made by chemical reactions in their bodies. Some use it to find mates. Some use it to scare off attackers or confuse them with a flash.

The [[@anglerfish|anglerfish]] dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, like a fishing rod with a lamp. Small fish swim closer to look, and the anglerfish snaps them up. Other fish have glowing spots on their bellies that match the faint light from above, so hunters below can't see their outline.

In 2022, a team from Australia and Japan lowered cameras into the Izu-Ogasawara Trench south of Japan. At 8,336 metres, they filmed a young snailfish, a small, pale fish with a big head and a body like soft jelly. It is the deepest fish ever recorded on video.

Snailfish look fragile, but that softness is their strength. They have no hard scales and no air bladder. Their skeletons are only partly hardened, so their bodies flex with the pressure instead of fighting it.

In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first people to reach Challenger Deep, in a craft called the Trieste. Through the window, they reported what they thought was a flatfish, though many scientists now doubt it. The film-maker James Cameron dived there alone in 2012.

Robotic landers and crewed dives since then have found life all the way to the bottom. There are amphipods the size of a thumb, sea cucumbers drifting over the mud, and giant single-celled creatures called xenophyophores. Scientists think most deep-sea [[species|species]] have never been seen by anyone at all.

text: Yes, the seas of the dinosaur age had real monsters. But they weren't dinosaurs. Dinosaurs lived on land. The giants of the sea were other kinds of [[reptile|reptiles]] that had moved back into the water.

There were three main groups. Ichthyosaurs looked a lot like dolphins. [[@marine-reptiles-plesiosaur|Plesiosaurs]] had four big flippers, and many had very [[@sauropod-necks|long necks]]. Mosasaurs were huge sea lizards with snapping jaws. Alongside them swam giant turtles and early [[@sharks-old|sharks]].
Like whales today, all of them breathed air. They had to come up to the surface to fill their lungs.

spots: Shaped like a dolphin. It gave birth to live babies in the water.
Long neck, four flippers, ‘flew’ through the water.
A giant sea lizard, related to today's monitor lizards and snakes.

quiz.reveal: Mosasaurs were lizards that took to the sea. Their skulls and jaws are a lot like those of monitor lizards and snakes, and like snakes they had extra joints in their jaws for gulping big prey.

d.try: Fill a bucket or a sink with water. Push your flat hand through it palm first, then again edge first. Feel how much easier the edge slides through. That is why dolphins, sharks and ichthyosaurs all ended up with the same smooth, pointed shape.
myth: The Loch Ness Monster might be a plesiosaur that survived.
Plesiosaurs died out 66 million years ago, and Loch Ness only filled with water after the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago. No search of the loch has ever found a large animal.

sec.t:
The name ichthyosaur means "fish lizard". They had pointed snouts, a fin on the back and a tail shaped like a crescent. Yet they [[evolve|evolved]] from four-legged reptiles that lived on land. This shows how the same problem, moving fast through water, can lead very different animals to the same shape. Scientists call it convergent [[evolution|evolution]].

Some ichthyosaurs had eyes as wide as a dinner plate, probably for hunting in dim, deep water. They didn't lay eggs on beaches. In Germany, [[fossil|fossils]] have been found of mothers that died while giving birth, with babies coming out tail first, just as baby dolphins do.

Mosasaurs came last and grew largest, with some reaching about 15 m, longer than a city bus. They had powerful tails, flippers and a second row of teeth on the roof of the mouth to grip slippery prey.

Their fossils turn up in surprising places. One of the first was dug out of a quarry near Maastricht in the Netherlands in the 1700s. In Kansas, in the middle of the USA, the rocks are full of mosasaurs and plesiosaurs. That is because a shallow sea once split North America in two.

India has its own sea monster too. In 2016, scientists found an ichthyosaur skeleton about 150 million years old near the village of Lodai in Kutch, Gujarat. It was the first one from that age found in India.

Ichthyosaurs died out about 90 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs. Plesiosaurs and mosasaurs lasted until 66 million years ago. Then [[@extinction|the asteroid]] that ended the age of dinosaurs wiped them out too.

Some sea reptiles did make it through, as you can read in [[@who-survived|who survived]]. Sea turtles and crocodiles are still with us. A 4 m sea turtle called Archelon, as long as a car, swam in the same seas as the mosasaurs. Its smaller relatives still come ashore on Indian beaches to lay their eggs, like the [[@sea-turtles|olive ridleys]] of Odisha.

text: Cheetahs went [[extinct|extinct]] in India by 1952.
Project Cheetah brought African cheetahs to Kuno National Park to help restore grassland wildlife.

It's an experiment. Some scientists support it; others worry about whether there's enough space and prey. It was the first time a large wild cat was moved from one continent to another to live in the wild.

events.d: Asiatic cheetahs once ran across India's grasslands. Kings even kept them for hunting.
India declared cheetahs extinct here, after hunting and the loss of grasslands.
Eight cheetahs flew from Namibia to Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh.
More arrived from South Africa, and the first cubs were born in India.
Some cheetahs have died. Scientists are learning what helps them survive here.

sec.t:
Asiatic cheetahs once ran across grasslands and open scrub from central India to Arabia. For centuries, Indian kings caught them to hunt [[@wild-blackbuck|blackbuck]] and deer. The Mughal emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] is said to have kept about a thousand at one time. Captured cheetahs rarely bred in captivity, so more and more had to be taken from the wild.

Hunting, the loss of grasslands to farms and the shrinking of their prey slowly emptied the land. In 1947, the Maharaja of Koriya, in present-day Chhattisgarh, is recorded as shooting three cheetahs at night. They are often described as the last confirmed wild cheetahs in India. In 1952, the government declared the animal extinct in the country.

The first years were difficult. Several adult cheetahs and many cubs died. Some deaths came from fights and from heat. Others were blamed on [[infection|infections]] under the [[@radio-invented|radio]] collars, as some cheetahs grew thick coats meant for an African winter and moisture got trapped beneath them.

Some cheetahs also wandered far outside the park, into farms and villages, and had to be caught and brought back. In 2025, a few were moved to a second home, the Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary, also in Madhya Pradesh. Scientists are learning what helps cheetahs survive here.

Supporters say cheetahs are a symbol for India's neglected grasslands. Protecting a big, eye-catching animal can also protect [[@wolves-india|wolves]], foxes, blackbuck, the great Indian bustard and the grasses themselves.

Critics point out that Kuno is much smaller than the vast open spaces where cheetahs roam in Africa. [[@leopards-cities|They worry about leopards]], which kill cheetahs and their cubs, and about too little prey. Some argue the money would do more good spent on animals already struggling in India. Both sides agree that the cheetahs' future depends on large, connected grasslands where people and wildlife can share the land.

The cheetah is the [[@fastest-animal|fastest land animal]], reaching about 100 km/h in short bursts. A deer or blackbuck that can run long enough usually escapes. Its spots break up its outline in dry grass, a different trick from a [[@tiger-stripes|tiger's stripes]]. If Project Cheetah works, some of those sprints may soon be happening on Indian grasslands again, as they did in Akbar's time.

text: Asiatic lions once lived across a huge stretch of the world, from the Middle East through Iran to much of northern and central India. Over the centuries, people hunted them, cleared their land for farms and killed the [[@deer-india|deer]] and antelope they ate. By the late 1800s, lions had vanished from everywhere except one patch of dry forest in Gujarat: Gir.

They survived there partly by luck and partly because the rulers of the region, the Nawabs of Junagadh, began protecting them in the early 1900s. After India's independence, Gir became a [[sanctuary|sanctuary]] in 1965.
From a few dozen lions, the population has grown to about 890 in the 2025 count. Every one of them lives in Gujarat.

st.prompt: Apart from zoos, where else in the world do wild Asiatic lions live today?
st.reveal: Every wild Asiatic lion lives in Gujarat, in and around Gir. Lions once lived across the Middle East and much of northern and central India, but hunting and farming wiped them out everywhere else.

facts: Gir and nearby parts of Saurashtra, Gujarat

sec.t:
Around 1900, some reports claimed fewer than 20 lions were left. Some historians think that figure was too low, and may even have been kept low on purpose to discourage hunters. Either way, the Asiatic lion came very close to vanishing.

British officers and Indian princes had shot lions for sport for decades, often in large numbers, and a lion skin was a prized trophy. Protection came just in time. Today there are more wild lions in Gujarat than at any time in over a century.

Gir is not empty of people. The Maldhari herders have lived inside the forest for generations, in small settlements called *nes*, grazing buffaloes and cows. Lions sometimes take their animals, and the government pays some compensation. Yet many Maldharis are proud of the lions and tolerate them as neighbours.

As their numbers grew, lions spread far beyond the forest. They now roam farmland, hills and even beaches along the coast of Saurashtra. People have filmed lions strolling past temples, crossing highways and resting in [[@mango-tree|mango]] orchards.

Having every lion in one place has a big weakness. In 2018, more than 20 lions in one part of Gir died within a few weeks, from a virus caught from dogs and a disease spread by ticks. A larger outbreak could hit the whole population.

In 2013, India's [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] ordered that some lions be moved to Kuno in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] to start a second population. That has not happened. Gujarat argues that its lions are thriving and already spreading into new areas. Many wildlife scientists say a home far away would be safer. Kuno later received [[@cheetah-return|cheetahs]] from Africa instead.

Lions have stood for strength and power in India for over 2,000 years. When India became a [[republic|republic]], it chose the lions carved on [[@ashoka|Emperor Ashoka's]] pillar at Sarnath as its emblem.

Those stone lions are Asiatic lions, carved when they still lived across much of the country. Today their real-life cousins have one forest to call home, and a country deciding where they should go next.

text: बिहू असम का लोकनृत्य है, जो बसंत के आने और अप्रैल के बीच में असमिया नए साल की शुरुआत की खुशी में नाचा जाता है। लड़के-लड़कियाँ टोलियों में नाचते हैं। लड़कियाँ कमर लचकाती हैं और हाथों को तेज़, लहराती मुद्राओं में घुमाती हैं, जबकि लड़के उछलते हैं और ढोल बजाते हैं। ताल तेज़ होती है, और नाचते-नाचते और तेज़ होती जाती है।

यह नाच रंगाली बिहू का है, जिसे बोहाग बिहू भी कहते हैं। असम के तीनों बिहू में यही सबसे खुशियों भरा है। *रंगाली* शब्द *रोंग* से बना है, जिसका मतलब है आनंद। यह तब आता है जब खेत बुवाई के लिए तैयार होते हैं, पेड़ों पर फूल खिलते हैं और पहली बारिश करीब होती है। हफ़्ते भर या उससे ज़्यादा, [[@northeast-india|पूर्वोत्तर भारत]] के गाँव और शहर ढोल की थाप से गूँजते रहते हैं।

sec.t:
बिहू की धड़कन है ढोल, पीपे जैसा [[@drums|ढोल]] जो कंधे से लटकाया जाता है और दोनों ओर से बजता है, एक तरफ़ डंडी से और दूसरी तरफ़ हाथ से। अच्छे ढोलिए उससे सरपट दौड़ते घोड़ों जैसी आवाज़ निकाल देते हैं।

फिर आता है पेपा, भैंस के सींग से बनी पीपनी। इसकी ऊँची, लहराती तान ढोल के शोर को चीरती हुई निकलती है। गोगोना बाँस से बना एक छोटा मुँह-बाजा है, जिसे होंठों से सटाकर छेड़ा जाता है। ताल नाम के मँजीरे लय बनाए रखते हैं, और चिरे हुए बाँस का खटका, टोका, सूखी खट-खट जोड़ता है।

यह सब सामने बैठकर, जीते-जागते बजाया जाता है। बिहू मंच पर आने से बहुत पहले गाँव का नाच था, इसलिए बजाने वाले और नाचने वाले एक-दूसरे से जोश लेते हुए साथ-साथ रफ़्तार बढ़ाते हैं।

बिहू किसानों के नाच के रूप में शुरू हुआ। बसंत अच्छी बारिश और अच्छी फ़सल की दुआ माँगने का समय था, और थोड़ी शर्म के साथ, जीवनसाथी ढूँढने का भी। बहुत-से बिहू [[folklore|लोकगीत]], जिन्हें *बिहुगीत* कहते हैं, प्यार, [[monsoon|मानसून]], ब्रह्मपुत्र नदी और खेतों के काम के बारे में हैं।

कहा जाता है कि लगभग 600 साल असम पर राज करने वाले [[@ahom-kingdom|अहोम राज्य]] के राजा बिहू नर्तकों को अपने शाही मैदानों में नाचने बुलाते थे। धीरे-धीरे गाँव का यह नाच राजदरबार का मनोरंजन भी बन गया।

गाँवों में आज भी रंगाली बिहू के दिनों में आदमियों की टोलियाँ, जिन्हें *हुसोरी* कहते हैं, घर-घर जाती हैं। यह एक पुरानी [[ritual|रीत]] है। वे हर आँगन में गाती हैं, परिवार को आने वाले साल का आशीर्वाद देती हैं और बदले में सुपारी, गमोसा या कुछ सिक्के पाती हैं। यह कुछ-कुछ वैसा ही है जैसे कई त्योहारों पर गाने-बजाने वाली टोलियाँ मोहल्ले में घर-घर घूमती हैं, बस यहाँ ढोल की धमक ज़्यादा है।

{{story:assam-tea}}

आज बिहू स्कूलों में, टीवी पर और शहरों के बड़े मंचों पर नाचा जाता है, जिन्हें *बिहुतोली* कहते हैं। दिल्ली, बेंगलुरु और अमेरिका में बसे असमिया परिवार हर अप्रैल अपनी-अपनी बिहू शामें मनाते हैं।

नाचने वाली लड़कियाँ आम तौर पर *मेखेला सादर* पहनती हैं, जो दो हिस्सों वाली पोशाक है। सबसे बढ़िया मेखेला सादर मूगा से बुने जाते हैं, एक सुनहरा [[@silk|रेशम]] जो लगभग सिर्फ़ असम में बनता है। मूगा कपड़ा इस बात के लिए मशहूर है कि हर धुलाई के साथ उसकी चमक और बढ़ जाती है। नर्तकियाँ अक्सर बालों में *कोपौ फूल* खोंसती हैं, यानी फ़ॉक्सटेल ऑर्किड।

लड़के *धोती* पहनते हैं, सिर या कमर पर *गमोसा* बाँधते हैं, और कभी-कभी छोटी जैकेट भी। गमोसा लाल किनारी वाला सफ़ेद सूती गमछा है। यह असम की पहचान में इतना रचा-बसा है कि मेहमानों को सम्मान के तौर पर भेंट किया जाता है।

13 अप्रैल 2023 को गुवाहाटी के एक स्टेडियम में 11,304 नर्तकों और ढोलवादकों ने एक साथ बिहू किया। गिनीज़ वर्ल्ड रिकॉर्ड्स ने इसे अब तक का सबसे बड़ा बिहू नृत्य माना, और बिहू ढोल के सबसे बड़े प्रदर्शन का एक दूसरा रिकॉर्ड भी बना। दर्शकों की सीटों से मैदान लाल और सुनहरे रंग का एक चलता-फिरता कालीन लग रहा था।

किसी पेड़ के नीचे नाचते चंद लोगों से यह बहुत लंबा सफ़र था। फिर भी कदम वही थे जो दादी-नानी गाँव के आँगनों में सिखाती हैं, और आज भी बारिश, धान और बदलते साल की [[rhythm|लय]] से बँधे हैं। अगर चाय के बागान [[@assam-tea|असम]] की सबसे मशहूर पहचान हैं, तो बिहू शायद उसकी सबसे ऊँची आवाज़ है।

text: Frank Lloyd Wright was an American architect who lived from 1867 to 1959. Over about 70 years he designed more than 1,000 buildings, and roughly 530 were actually built. They include houses, churches, offices and one of the world's most unusual museums.

Wright believed buildings should fit their surroundings, as if they had grown there. He called this "organic [[architecture|architecture]]". His homes are often long and low, hugging the ground, with big overhanging roofs, natural wood and stone, and rooms that flow into each other. His most famous house, Fallingwater, sits right over a waterfall in the woods of Pennsylvania.

sec.t:
Wright was born in Richland Center, a small town in Wisconsin. When he was a boy, his mother gave him a set of Froebel blocks. These were smooth maple cubes, cylinders and triangles invented by a German teacher, Friedrich Froebel, to help small children learn about shapes.

Wright later said the blocks shaped how he thought about buildings for the rest of his life. The love of building toys ran in the family. His son John invented Lincoln Logs, the notched wooden logs that he created around 1916, long before plastic [[@lego|LEGO]] bricks existed.

In the 1930s, the Kaufmann family of Pittsburgh asked Wright to design a weekend house near a waterfall on a stream called Bear Run. They expected a house with a view of the falls. Wright put the house right on top of them.

Fallingwater, built between 1936 and 1939, has wide concrete terraces that stretch out over the stream, held up only at one end. This is called a cantilever, like a diving board. The stone floor of the living room is built around boulders from the site, and steps lead down to the water. Over the years the terraces sagged and needed major repairs. Today the house is a museum, and visitors come from all over the world.

Wright's last great building was the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in [[@new-york|New York]]. It is shaped like a giant white spiral, wider at the top than at the bottom. Visitors take a lift to the top and walk slowly down a long ramp that curves around an open centre, looking at art as they go.

Wright worked on the design for about 16 years. The museum opened in October 1959, six months after he died at the age of 91.

Wright could be difficult. He was famously proud, often went over budget and sometimes ignored what his clients asked for. Several of his buildings had leaking roofs, and he was known for brushing off the complaints. His private life was often in the newspapers.

Still, his influence is everywhere. The open-plan living room, where kitchen, dining and sitting areas flow together, owes a lot to him. In 2019, UNESCO listed eight of his buildings, including Fallingwater and the Guggenheim, as a World Heritage Site.

sec.t:
हर पत्थर का बर्ताव अलग होता है। सेलखड़ी इतनी नरम है कि नाख़ून से खुरच जाए। एलाबस्टर और कुछ बलुआ पत्थर भी नरम होते हैं। संगमरमर थोड़ा सख़्त है, और उसके दाने बारीक और एक जैसे होते हैं, इसलिए उस पर बारीक काम और चमक दोनों ख़ूब खिलते हैं।

[[granite|ग्रेनाइट]] और [[basalt|बेसाल्ट]] सबसे सख़्त पत्थरों में हैं। उन्हें हाथ से तराशने में ग़ज़ब का धीरज चाहिए। भारत के बहुत से मंदिर-मूर्तिकार आज भी ग्रेनाइट में काम करते हैं, और दक्षिण भारत की [[@temple-sculpture|मंदिर मूर्तियाँ]] दिखाती हैं कि वह धीरज क्या कर सकता है।

तराशने वाले शुरू करने से पहले छिपी ख़ामियाँ ढूँढते हैं। वे पत्थर को ठोककर सुनते हैं। साफ़ खनक का मतलब है ठोस पत्थर। धप्प-सी भोथरी आवाज़ का मतलब हो सकता है कि अंदर दरार है।

हाथ से तराशने वाले ज़्यादातर कारीगर एक मुगरी और स्टील की कई छेनियाँ इस्तेमाल करते हैं। नुकीली छेनी, जिसकी धार कील जैसी होती है, बड़े-बड़े टुकड़े तोड़ती है। दाँतेदार छेनी, जिसमें दाँतों की एक कतार होती है, सतह को आकार देती है और छोटी-छोटी खाँचें छोड़ती है। चपटी छेनी उसे चिकना करती है। फिर आती हैं रेतियाँ, यानी खुरदुरी घिसनियाँ, और आख़िर में रेगमाल या घिसाई के पत्थर।

आज बहुत से मूर्तिकार हवा के दबाव से चलने वाले हथौड़े और हीरे के ब्लेड वाली बिजली की ग्राइंडर भी इस्तेमाल करते हैं, ख़ासकर सख़्त पत्थर के लिए। बड़े पत्थर-कारख़ानों में कंप्यूटर से चलने वाली मशीनें मोटा आकार काट देती हैं, और फिर कलाकार हाथ से उसे पूरा करता है।

1501 में इटली के फ़्लोरेंस शहर में [[@michelangelo|माइकलएंजेलो]] नाम के एक नौजवान मूर्तिकार को संगमरमर का एक विशाल, ऊँचा टुकड़ा सौंपा गया। दूसरे मूर्तिकारों ने दशकों पहले उस पर काम शुरू किया था और फिर छोड़ दिया था। वह लगभग 25 साल से एक कारख़ाने के आँगन में पड़ा था।

लगभग तीन साल में उन्होंने उसे डेविड में बदल दिया, बाइबल का वह नौजवान नायक। यह [[sculpture|मूर्ति]] लगभग 5.17 मीटर ऊँची है, किसी बड़े आदमी से लगभग तीन गुना। तराशे जाने से पहले ही फ़्लोरेंस के लोग उस टुकड़े को "दैत्य" कहने लगे थे।

माइकलएंजेलो कहा करते थे कि आकृति पत्थर के अंदर पहले से मौजूद थी। उनका काम बस उसे आज़ाद करना था।

{{story:mount-rushmore}}

कर्नाटक के श्रवणबेलगोला में गोम्मटेश्वर की मूर्ति खड़ी है, जिन्हें बाहुबली भी कहते हैं। वे जैन धर्म में पूजनीय हैं, जिसकी शिक्षा [[@mahavira|महावीर]] ने दी। लगभग 983 ईस्वी में पहाड़ी की चोटी पर ग्रेनाइट की एक ही चट्टान से तराशी गई यह मूर्ति लगभग 17 मीटर ऊँची है। यानी लगभग पाँच मंज़िला इमारत जितनी।

लगभग हर बारह साल में महामस्तकाभिषेक नाम का एक अनुष्ठान होता है। पुजारी एक ऊँचे मचान से मूर्ति के सिर पर दूध, केसर और दूसरी चढ़ावे की चीज़ें उँडेलते हैं।

[[@taj-mahal|ताजमहल]] का सफ़ेद संगमरमर राजस्थान के मकराना से आया था, जहाँ सदियों से संगमरमर निकाला जाता रहा है। वहाँ के कारीगर आज भी हाथ से पच्चीकारी और जाली काटते हैं, और उनमें से बहुत से ऐसे परिवारों से हैं जो पीढ़ियों से यही काम करते आए हैं।

पत्थर के बड़े कामों में अक्सर वही औज़ार इस्तेमाल हुए जो सबसे कारगर हों। अमेरिका के साउथ डकोटा में माउंट रशमोर पर 1927 से 1941 के बीच मज़दूरों ने लगभग 90% चट्टान डायनामाइट से उड़ाई, फिर ड्रिल और हाथ के औज़ारों से काम पूरा किया।

छोटे काम आज भी ज़्यादातर हाथ से होते हैं। कोई कारीगर पूरा दिन किसी चोगे की एक सिलवट या होंठ के एक घुमाव पर लगा सकता है। पत्थर पर स्टील की ठक-ठक, एक के बाद एक, हर जगह एक जैसी सुनाई देती है, चाहे मामल्लपुरम की कोई कार्यशाला हो, इटली का कैरारा हो या न्यूयॉर्क का कोई मूर्तिकला स्टूडियो।

text: In 2014, India's Mars Orbiter Mission, nicknamed Mangalyaan, slipped into [[orbit|orbit]] around Mars on the very first try. No Asian country had reached Mars orbit before. It cost about ₹450 crore, roughly $74 million at the time. The Hollywood film *Gravity*, about astronauts in trouble, cost about $100 million to make.

ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation, does this again and again. Its secret is a mix of things. Its engineers earn less than those in rich countries. It reuses designs from one mission to the next and builds very few spare test models. And it has a habit of solving problems with clever thinking rather than more money.

st.prompt: To save fuel on the way to Mars, what did ISRO's Mangalyaan do before heading off?

options.t: Looped around Earth several times, raising its orbit step by step
Waited on the Moon to refuel
Launched from a mountain top to be closer to space

st.reveal: India's PSLV rocket was too small to fling Mangalyaan straight to Mars. So the spacecraft circled Earth for about a month, firing its engine at the right moments to stretch its orbit. Then it slingshotted off towards Mars.

d.try: Plan a pretend space mission with ₹100 of play money. List what you need (rocket, fuel, camera, team snacks) and give each a price. Then try to cut your costs by a third without dropping anything important. That is roughly the puzzle ISRO's engineers solve every day.
myth: ISRO's missions are cheap because they use poor-quality parts.

The savings come mostly from lower salaries and local costs, reusing tested designs, and building fewer test models. ISRO's rockets and spacecraft meet tough international standards, and many countries pay ISRO to launch their satellites.

sec.t:
Here are some numbers to feel. India's Department of Space got about ₹13,700 crore in the 2026–27 [[@budgets|budget]]. That is roughly $1.5 billion. NASA, the US space agency, gets about $25 billion a year, about sixteen times more.

Yet ISRO has landed [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] near the Moon's south pole (2023), sent a probe to study the Sun called Aditya-L1, and once launched 104 satellites on a single rocket, in February 2017. That was a world record until a SpaceX rocket carried 143 in 2021. Chandrayaan-3 cost about ₹615 crore, which is less than many big Bollywood and Hollywood films. Mangalyaan travelled about 67 crore km to reach Mars. Divide the cost by the distance and you get under ₹7 a kilometre, less than the meter charges in a Bengaluru autorickshaw.

Building a spacecraft usually means making several practice versions first, to test in shaking machines and heat chambers. ISRO often builds fewer of these, testing parts carefully instead. It reuses proven designs: Mangalyaan was based on a satellite frame ISRO had already flown many times.

Indian-made parts are cheaper than imported ones. Engineers' salaries are much lower than in the USA or Europe. And clever planning saves fuel, which saves money. Mangalyaan looped around Earth for weeks, stretching its orbit each time, before heading to Mars. A bigger, costlier rocket could have gone straight there.

Time was squeezed too. The Mars team built Mangalyaan in about 15 months, partly because Earth and Mars line up well for a cheap trip only once every 26 months or so. Miss the window and you wait two years. Working to a hard deadline left little room for expensive extras.

Not everyone thinks the "low-cost" label is all good. Some Indian scientists say ISRO needs more money, not praise for spending less, to build bigger rockets and do more research. Smaller budgets can also mean slower progress: India's crewed mission, [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]], has taken years longer than first planned.

ISRO has had failures too. The Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-2 crashed in 2019. Engineers studied what went wrong, and four years later Chandrayaan-3 landed safely. Now India is working on rockets that can fly more than once, the same idea that has made [[@reusable-rockets|reusable rockets]] the biggest money saver in spaceflight today.

text: Firefighters put out fires, but that is only the start. They rescue people trapped in buildings, cars and floodwater. They deal with gas leaks and chemical spills. In many places they are the first to arrive at medical emergencies. In the USA, in fact, medical calls make up most of the work, far more than fires. They also inspect buildings for fire safety and visit schools to teach children what to do if a fire breaks out.
They work in shifts so that a fire station is ready day and night. When an alarm comes in, a crew can be dressed, on the fire engine and on its way within a minute or two.

st.prompt: A fire needs three things to keep burning. Firefighters try to take away at least one. Which three?
st.reveal: This is called the fire triangle. Water cools the heat, clearing away dry plants removes fuel, and foam or a blanket cuts off oxygen. Take away any one side and the fire goes out.

myth: Firefighters spend nearly all their time putting out fires.

Fires are only part of the job. Firefighters also rescue people from crashes, floods and collapsed buildings, help with medical emergencies, check buildings for fire safety and teach people how to prevent fires.

sec.t:
Every fire needs three things: heat, fuel and oxygen. Firefighters call this the fire triangle, and their job is to break it. Spraying water cools the fire down. Foam smothers the flames and cuts off oxygen. In a [[@forest-fires|forest fire]], crews may clear a strip of land so that the flames run out of fuel.

Different fires need different tools. Water is dangerous on burning oil or electrical equipment, so firefighters may use foam, powder or [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] instead. Understanding [[@fire-burns|what fire is]] is the first thing trainees learn.

sec.h: Firefighting in India and the USA
sec.t:
In India, fire services are run by state governments and cities. You can reach them on 101 or on the general emergency number 112. Officers are trained at places like the National Fire Service College in Nagpur. In 2002, Harshini Kanhekar became the first woman to join that college's firefighting course, and many women now serve.

In the USA, there are more than a million firefighters, and most of them are volunteers, especially in small towns. One of the first volunteer fire companies in America was started in Philadelphia in 1736 by [[@benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]]. He had seen how quickly fires spread through wooden towns. Members kept leather buckets at home and promised to run to any fire, day or night.

On 14 April 1944, a cargo ship called the Fort Stikine caught fire in Bombay's docks. It was carrying cotton, gold and a large load of explosives. Firefighters were battling the blaze when two huge explosions tore through the docks. Hundreds of people died, including 66 firefighters.

The blasts were so strong that burning cotton and debris landed far across the city. Since then, India has marked 14 April as National Fire Service Day, followed by a Fire Service Week when fire stations hold drills and teach fire safety.

Firefighters say the best fire is one that never starts. Simple habits help: never play with matches or lighters, keep things that burn away from stoves, and don't overload plug sockets. Working [[@smoke-alarms|smoke alarms]] give families precious extra minutes to get out. If you ever smell smoke or see fire, get out first, stay out, and call for help from a safe place.

text: A game designer decides how a game works. They choose the goal, the rules, the challenges and the rewards. They decide what happens when you press a button, how hard the third level should be and what makes a player want to try just one more time.

Designers work with programmers, artists, writers and musicians. There is no single path into the job. Many studied computer science, art or design, and some studied something else entirely. What nearly all of them have in common is that they started young, by making small games of their own and showing them to other people.

st.prompt: A designer has a new idea for a game level. What do most professionals do first?

options.t: Build a rough version and watch people try it
Spend a year making it look beautiful
Ask a computer to decide if it is fun

st.reveal: A rough prototype, often with plain boxes instead of art, shows quickly whether an idea is fun. Watching real players reveals where they get stuck or bored. Designers then fix and test again, many times over.

d.try: Make a one-page board game. Draw a path of 30 squares, add three squares with a twist (such as "swap places with another player"), and play it with someone. Afterwards, ask what was boring and what was exciting, change one rule, and play again.
myth: Game designers spend their days playing games.

They play a lot, but most of their time goes on writing ideas down, building rough versions, testing them with players and fixing what doesn't work. Much of the job is careful problem-solving and teamwork.

sec.t:
The American designer Sid Meier, who made the *Civilization* games, has described a game as "a series of interesting decisions". A designer's job is to make those decisions interesting. Should you take the safe path or the risky one? Spend your coins now or save them?

On a big team, there are many kinds of designer. A level designer builds the maps and puzzles. A systems designer balances numbers, such as how much damage a sword does. A narrative designer works on story and characters. In a tiny studio, one person might do all three.

The most important part of the job is playtesting. A designer sits behind a player and watches, without helping. Where does the player get lost? When do they look bored? What makes them laugh or sit up?

Often the answers are surprising. A puzzle the designer thought was easy might stump everyone. A small jump that was added as a joke might become everyone's favourite part. The team makes changes and tests again, sometimes hundreds of times before a game is finished.

Shigeru Miyamoto grew up in a small town near Kyoto in Japan. He has said that wandering the hills, woods and caves there, and the excitement of finding something unexpected, fed into *The Legend of Zelda*. Tetris was made in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov, a computer scientist in Moscow, who loved a puzzle with shapes made of squares.

Indian designers draw on their own stories. *Raji: An Ancient Epic*, made by a studio in Pune and released in 2020, sends a young girl through a world shaped by Indian myths and temple art. Good [[@video-game-music|music]] and sound also shape how a game feels, so designers work closely with composers.

You don't have to wait until you're grown up. Free tools such as Scratch let you make games with drag-and-drop blocks, and many teenagers move on to engines like Godot or Unity. Learning a little [[@programming|programming]] helps, but so do maths, art, writing and even psychology.

Game jams are events where people make a whole game in a weekend around a theme. They work much like [[@hackathons|hackathons]] and are a fast way to learn. Keep your games small and finish them. A short game that works teaches you more than a huge one that never ends.

Designers also play widely: card games, sports, puzzles and games they don't like. Each one shows a different way to make a decision interesting.

text: Pokémon took off because it mixed three things children already loved: collecting, battling and trading with friends. You catch creatures, train them, and swap them with other players to fill your Pokédex, a kind of catalogue.

The first games came out in Japan in 1996 for Nintendo's Game Boy. Within a few years there was a cartoon, a trading card game, films and toys, each pulling fans into the others. Pokémon is often listed as the highest-earning media franchise in history, though such totals are rough estimates. The idea behind it began with a boy who loved bugs.

options.t: Some Pokémon appeared in only one version, so players had to trade
One version was for boys and one for girls
The green version was a cheaper copy

st.reveal: Each version had Pokémon the other lacked. To catch all 151, you had to link your Game Boy to a friend's with a cable and swap. The games turned collecting into something you did with other people.

myth: Pikachu has a black tip on its tail.
It never has. Pikachu's ears are black-tipped, but its tail is yellow with a brown patch at the base. So many people remember it wrongly that it is often given as an example of a shared false memory.

sec.t:
The two first versions, Red and Green, each had Pokémon the other was missing. That simple trick meant no one could finish alone. Children had to meet, talk and trade, and the game spread through playgrounds by word of mouth.

The creatures also had types, like water, fire and grass, which work a bit like rock, paper, scissors. Water beats fire, fire beats grass, and grass beats water. Easy to learn, but with 151 Pokémon there were endless combinations to argue over.

sec.h: From Game Boy to TV screens
sec.t:
In 1997 an anime series started in Japan, following a boy called Satoshi (renamed Ash in English) and his Pikachu. It reached American TV in 1998, and the trading card game soon followed. Each part fed the others: the cartoon made you want the cards, and the cards sent you back to the game.

In India, Hindi-dubbed episodes ran on channels including [[@cartoon-network-india|Cartoon Network]] and later Hungama. For many Indian children, the cartoon came first, years before they ever touched a Game Boy.

In 2016, the company Niantic released Pokémon Go for phones. It used [[@gps-how|GPS]] and the phone's camera to place Pokémon in the real world, in parks, at bus stops and outside temples. Millions of people walked around their towns staring at their screens.

The game had problems too. Some players wandered into unsafe places or private property while chasing a rare creature, and some cities asked for game spots to be moved.

Many crazes vanish after a few years. Pokémon kept adding new regions and new creatures, and there are now more than 1,000. Each new pair of games brings fresh creatures to learn, which gives older fans a reason to come back and younger ones a fair place to start. Parents who played Red and Green in the 1990s now play with their own children.

The heart of it has not changed much: a world full of creatures waiting to be found, and someone to show them to.

text: Dolls are some of the oldest toys in the world. Children in ancient Egypt, Rome, China and the Indus Valley played with figures made of clay, wood, cloth or bone. For thousands of years, most dolls were handmade at home or by local craftspeople.

In the 1800s, factories in Germany and France began making dolls with china heads and glass eyes. Then came rubber and plastic. In 1959, an American company launched Barbie, a grown-up fashion doll that changed the toy business.

Today dolls come in every shape, skin colour and job, from astronauts to doctors. They still tell us what each age thought children should dream about. Look at a shelf of dolls from different centuries and you are looking at a history of clothes, jobs and family life.

st.reveal: "Miss Astronaut" Barbie came out in 1965, four years before people landed on the Moon. The first American woman in space, Sally Ride, did not fly until 1983.

d.try: Make a simple doll from a clothes peg, scraps of cloth and wool. Then make a second one that shows a job you might like to do one day. Notice how much a doll's clothes and tools tell you about what its maker thought was important.
myth: Dolls have always been toys mostly meant for girls.

In many cultures and times, dolls and figures were shared by children of all kinds, or used in festivals and ceremonies. Toy makers in the 1960s even called boy-targeted dolls "action figures" to sell them, and the line between them is a marketing choice.

sec.t:
[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found small clay figures, animals on wheels and toy carts in the old [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], from about 4,500 years ago. Some animal figures even have heads that nod when you pull a string. Ancient Egyptians buried wooden "paddle dolls" with painted faces and long strings of beads for hair.

In Rome, a girl named Crepereia Tryphaena was buried in the 100s CE with an ivory doll whose arms and legs could bend at the joints. It was found in 1889, still with tiny jewellery. Not every ancient figure was a toy, though. Some were used in religious [[ritual|rituals]], and experts often argue over which was which.

Many cultures display dolls on special days. In Japan, families set out tiered shelves of royal Hina dolls for Hinamatsuri, or Girls' Day, on 3 March. In south India, many homes arrange steps of dolls called golu or bommai kolu during Navaratri, showing gods, saints, animals and everyday village scenes.

Indian craft towns have their own traditions. [[@channapatna-toys|Channapatna]] in Karnataka makes smooth wooden dolls coloured with natural dyes. Kondapalli in Andhra Pradesh carves figures from soft, light wood.

In Russia, the first matryoshka, or nesting doll, was made in the 1890s. Each doll opens to reveal a smaller one inside, sometimes eight or more. The first set showed a girl in a headscarf holding a rooster, with her family tucked inside her.

{{story:art-toy-making-kondapalli}}

Ruth Handler, who started the toy company Mattel with her husband, noticed her daughter Barbara playing with paper dolls of grown-up women. Most dolls then were babies. Handler wanted a doll that let girls picture adult lives. She was partly inspired by a German doll called Bild Lilli.

Barbie was launched on 9 March 1959 at a toy fair in New York. Her boyfriend, Ken, named after Handler's son, arrived in 1961. Barbie quickly gained hundreds of outfits and jobs, from nurse to pilot to news reporter. In 1965 there was "Miss Astronaut" Barbie, long before the first American woman in space. You can meet the real pioneers in [[@women-in-space|women in space]].

Barbie has always had critics. Many people said her very thin body and tiny feet were impossible in real life, and might make children unhappy with their own bodies. Others said she showed girls they could do any job.

Mattel has changed her over time. A Black doll named Barbie came out in 1980. In 2016 the company added tall, petite and curvy body types. Later dolls included wheelchair users and dolls with hearing aids.

In the US, action figures like GI Joe arrived in 1964. Toy companies avoided the word "doll" to sell them to boys. And the strangest part? Children's playthings have changed with every new material and idea, as you can trace in [[@toys-history|the history of toys]].

text: The Special Olympics is a worldwide sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities. An intellectual disability means a person learns and understands things more slowly than most people, and may need help with some everyday tasks.
Special Olympics athletes train all year in sports like athletics, swimming, football, basketball and bocce, an Italian bowling game. They compete in local, national and world games.
Its spirit is in the athlete oath, spoken at every event: "Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt."

st.prompt: In a Special Olympics swimming final, who gets an award?
st.reveal: The top three get gold, silver and bronze medals, and everyone else in the final gets a ribbon for their place. The idea is that taking part and trying your hardest deserves to be recognised.

myth: The Special Olympics and the Paralympics are the same thing.

They are separate movements. The Paralympics are for elite athletes with mainly physical or visual impairments, and only the fastest qualify. The Special Olympics are for people with intellectual disabilities at every level of ability, with training all year round.

sec.t:
In the early 1960s, people with intellectual disabilities were often kept out of sight. Many lived in large institutions and had little chance to play sports or even go to school.

Eunice Kennedy Shriver thought that was wrong. Her own sister, Rosemary, had an intellectual disability. In 1962 Shriver opened a summer day camp in the backyard of her home in Maryland, in the USA. She called it Camp Shriver. Children came to swim, ride horses, kick balls and climb.

The children did far more than many experts expected. Shriver became convinced that sport could change how the world saw people with intellectual disabilities.

Special Olympics does something unusual before a competition. Athletes are first timed or tested, and then placed in small groups called divisions with others of a similar ability. A runner who takes 20 seconds for a race won't be up against one who takes 40 seconds.

This makes every race close and exciting. An athlete with less experience has as much chance of winning gold in their division as a fast one in theirs.

Everyone who finishes is recognised. The top three get medals, and the others in each final get ribbons.

Special Olympics also runs Unified Sports. Here, people with and without intellectual disabilities play on the same team. A Unified team mixes players with and without intellectual disabilities, often in roughly equal numbers, all of a similar skill level.

Teammates train and compete as equals. Schools in many countries now run Unified clubs, and friendships often carry on off the field. This is part of a bigger idea, [[@disabilities-inclusion|inclusion]], which means building a world where everyone can take part.

India's programme, Special Olympics Bharat, trains hundreds of thousands of athletes across the country. Indian athletes have brought home large hauls of medals from World Games, in sports such as athletics, cycling, roller skating and powerlifting.

Some Indian athletes have travelled abroad for the first time to compete. For their families, seeing them on a podium with the national flag can be as big a moment as any cricket victory.

sec.h: How it differs from the Paralympics
sec.t:
People often mix up the Special Olympics and the [[@paralympics|Paralympics]]. The Paralympics are held right after the [[@olympics|Olympics]], in the same city. They are for top athletes, mostly with physical or visual impairments, and only the very best qualify, just as in the Olympics.

The Special Olympics are for people with intellectual disabilities of every ability level. A beginner and a world-class athlete are both welcome. The goal is to give everyone the chance to train, compete and be cheered on, however fast or slow they are.

sec.t:
हर हाथ में 27 हड्डियाँ होती हैं और हर पैर में 26। यानी हाथों और पैरों में मिलाकर 100 से ज़्यादा हड्डियाँ, पूरे [[skeleton|कंकाल]] की आधी से भी ज़्यादा। इन्हीं छोटी-छोटी हड्डियों की वजह से तुम्हारी उँगलियाँ पेंसिल पकड़ पाती हैं और पैर ऊबड़-खाबड़ सड़क पर संभल पाते हैं।

सबसे लंबी हड्डी फ़ीमर है, जो जाँघ में होती है। यह तुम्हारी लंबाई की लगभग एक-चौथाई होती है। सबसे छोटी है स्टेपीज़, जो कान के अंदर गहराई में होती है। यह चावल के एक दाने से भी छोटी है। इसका काम आवाज़ की [[vibration|कंपन]] को अंदरूनी कान तक पहुँचाना है।

हड्डियाँ ठोस दिखती हैं, पर ये ज़िंदा [[tissue|ऊतक]] हैं। इनकी सख़्त बाहरी परत ज़्यादातर कैल्शियम फ़ॉस्फ़ेट नाम के खनिज से बनी है। इसके साथ [[collagen|कोलेजन]] नाम का एक मज़बूत, थोड़ा लचीला प्रोटीन बुना होता है। खनिज हड्डी को सख़्त बनाता है। कोलेजन उसे काँच की तरह चटकने से बचाता है।

कई हड्डियों के अंदर स्पंज जैसी हल्की, मधुमक्खी के छत्ते जैसी बनावट होती है। कुछ के खोखले बीच में नरम गूदा, यानी मैरो, भरा होता है। लाल मैरो तुम्हारे [[@blood|खून]] की कोशिकाएँ बनाता है, हर सेकंड लाखों।

ख़ास कोशिकाएँ हड्डी को लगातार घोलती और फिर से बनाती रहती हैं। जब कोई हड्डी टूटती है, तो यही कोशिकाएँ टूटी जगह पर नई हड्डी बना देती हैं। इसीलिए प्लास्टर का काम बस टुकड़ों को हिलने से रोकना होता है।

{{story:x-rays}}

1895 में जर्मन वैज्ञानिक विल्हेम रॉन्टजन ने ऐसी अदृश्य किरणें खोजीं जो त्वचा के आर-पार निकल जाती थीं, पर हड्डी उन्हें रोक लेती थी। उन्होंने इन्हें [[@x-rays|एक्स-रे]] नाम दिया, क्योंकि गणित में X किसी अनजानी चीज़ के लिए लिखा जाता है। उनकी शुरुआती तस्वीरों में से एक में उनकी पत्नी आना बर्था के हाथ की हड्डियाँ दिख रही थीं, और एक उँगली के चारों ओर शादी की अँगूठी हवा में तैरती-सी लग रही थी। कुछ ही महीनों में दुनिया भर के डॉक्टर टूटी हड्डियाँ देखने के लिए एक्स-रे का इस्तेमाल करने लगे।

हड्डियाँ जितना काम करती हैं, उतनी मज़बूत होती हैं। दौड़ना, कूदना और वज़न उठाना उन्हें और खनिज जमा करने पर मजबूर करता है। [[@milk|दूध]], दही, रागी और हरी पत्तेदार सब्ज़ियों से मिलने वाला कैल्शियम इसमें मदद करता है। विटामिन डी भी, जो धूप लगने पर तुम्हारी त्वचा खुद बनाती है।

अंतरिक्ष में हड्डियाँ आलसी हो जाती हैं। तैरते हुए अंतरिक्ष यात्रियों की टाँगों पर कोई वज़न नहीं पड़ता, इसलिए उनकी हड्डियों से खनिज घटने लगता है। नासा ने पाया है कि लंबे मिशन पर गए यात्रियों की कुछ हड्डियों का वज़न हर महीने लगभग 1% तक घट सकता है, अगर वे रोज़ जमकर [[@exercise|कसरत]] न करें।

दाँत हड्डी जैसे दिखते हैं, पर हड्डी नहीं हैं। तुम्हारी नाक और कानों के ऊपरी हिस्से को [[cartilage|उपास्थि]] आकार देती है, जो सख़्त तो है पर मुड़ जाती है। बच्चों में उपास्थि ज़्यादा होती है, और बड़े होते-होते इसका बहुत-सा हिस्सा हड्डी बन जाता है। लंबी हड्डियों के सिरों के पास की ग्रोथ प्लेटें भी उपास्थि की होती हैं। जब ये आख़िरकार हड्डी बन जाती हैं, आम तौर पर किशोर उम्र के आख़िर में, तो तुम्हारी [[@growing-taller|लंबाई बढ़ना]] बंद हो जाती है।

शरीर के न रहने के बहुत बाद तक हड्डियाँ बची रहती हैं। [[@mystery-roopkund|पुराने कंकाल]] वैज्ञानिकों को बताते हैं कि लोग क्या खाते थे, कितने लंबे थे और उन्हें कौन सी चोटें लगी थीं। लाखों-करोड़ों सालों में ज़मीन में दबी हड्डियाँ पत्थर तक बन सकती हैं। डायनासोर के बारे में हम इसी तरह जानते हैं।

text: A placebo is a pretend treatment, such as a sugar pill or a salt-water injection, with no medicine in it. Yet when people believe they're getting real medicine, many of them feel better. Their pain eases, their sickness settles or they feel less tired. This is the placebo effect.

It happens because your [[@brain-works|brain]] is always predicting what will happen next. If it expects relief, it can turn down pain signals and release its own calming chemicals. The word comes from Latin and means "I shall please".
The effect is real, but it has limits. A placebo can change how you feel. It cannot kill germs or repair a torn muscle.

Placebos can cause real changes in the brain, such as the release of the body's own painkillers. They mostly change how symptoms feel, though, and they can't cure an infection or heal a broken bone.

sec.t:
In 1978, three scientists in San Francisco studied people who had just had a wisdom tooth pulled. Some were given a fake painkiller and said they felt better. Then the researchers gave them naloxone, a drug that blocks the body's natural painkillers, called endorphins. The relief faded.

That was a big clue. The fake pill had nothing in it, but believing in it had made the brain release real chemicals. Later brain scans showed areas that handle [[@pain|pain]] becoming quieter when people expected relief.

Expectation also works the other way. If people are warned that a pill may cause headaches, some get headaches even when the pill is fake. This is called the nocebo effect, from a Latin word meaning "I shall harm".

When scientists test a new medicine, they usually split volunteers into two groups. One group gets the real drug and the other gets an identical-looking placebo. Ideally nobody, not even the doctors, knows who got which until the end. This is called a double-blind trial.

If the medicine group does clearly better, the drug works. If both groups improve equally, the improvement probably came from expectation, from time passing or from people getting better on their own. That last part matters. Colds clear up, sore muscles heal and bad days pass. Some of what looks like a placebo effect is simply the body doing its normal job, which is why experts argue about how big the effect really is.

Researchers have noticed some odd patterns. Fake injections often seem to work better than fake pills. Branded-looking packets can do better than plain ones. In one study at Harvard in 2010, patients with a stomach condition were openly told their pills were placebos, and many still felt better.

None of this means you should swap medicine for sugar. Placebos don't shrink tumours or cure [[infection|infections]], and anyone who feels unwell should talk to a parent or a doctor. What placebos do show is how tightly the mind and body are wired together.

text: People can live under the sea, but only in small numbers and not for long. For more than 60 years, scientists have stayed in underwater bases for days or weeks at a time. Some people have lasted months. But a full city under the waves, with schools, shops and parks, has never been built.

The reasons are simple. Water is heavy, and it pushes hard on everything below it. Sea water is cold, salty and dark further down. Every breath of air, every drop of fresh water and every light bulb has to be supplied from somewhere.
Engineers still dream about it, though, and some plans are moving forward.

sec.t:
At sea level, the air above you presses on every part of your body. You don't notice because you are used to it. Go 10 metres underwater and the weight of the water doubles that pressure. At 20 metres it triples.

This is why divers' ears hurt as they go down. It is also why deep-sea [[@submarines|submarines]] have thick, round hulls. Humans can cope with a few [[atmosphere|atmospheres]] if they breathe air at the same pressure. But their bodies soak up extra gas, as you can read in [[@diving-body|what diving does to your body]].

That causes a problem when you come back up. If the pressure drops too fast, gas bubbles form in the blood, a dangerous condition called the bends. People who live in a deep [[habitat|habitat]] must decompress slowly, sometimes for most of a day, before they can safely return.

In 1963, the French explorer Jacques Cousteau set up Conshelf II in the Red Sea. Five men lived there for a month, with a garage for a small submarine. Around the same time, the US Navy tested its own Sealab habitats.

Today, the best-known base is Aquarius, about 19 metres deep off the coast of Florida. Scientists and astronauts-in-training live there for missions of about ten days. They study coral reefs, and NASA has used it to practise for life in space. When a mission ends, the crew spend about 17 hours decompressing before they swim back up.

In 2023, an American researcher lived for 100 days in a small underwater lodge in Florida. In January 2025, a German engineer named Rüdiger Koch broke that record by spending 120 days in a capsule off the coast of Panama.

{{story:ocean-exploration-india}}

A real underwater city would face huge challenges. Walls and windows must hold back the sea for decades without leaking. Salt water eats away at metal. Air must be cleaned of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] all the time, and the damp inside encourages mould.

Power and food are harder still. Ideas include using ocean currents or waves for electricity, and growing seaweed and fish around the base. Fresh water could come from removing salt from sea water, which already happens in many dry countries.

Living without sunlight for months can also affect sleep and mood. Astronauts face the same problem, which is why the challenges are similar to building [[@mars-colonies|colonies on Mars]]. At least under the sea, help is a few hours away rather than months.

You can already eat lunch underwater. Ithaa, a restaurant in the [[@maldives|Maldives]], sits about 5 metres below the surface inside a curved glass tunnel. A restaurant in Norway, opened in 2019, has a giant window looking onto the sea.

Engineers have drawn up bigger designs. A Japanese company has proposed a spiral city plunging deep into the ocean, and a new research base called Proteus is planned off the Caribbean island of Curaçao. None of these are built yet.

Some people see the ocean as a place to escape crowded land or [[@sea-level-rise|rising seas]]. Others say it would always be easier to build on land. And the strangest part? We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of most of our own sea floor.

text: A video call does five jobs at once, over and over, very fast. Your camera takes about 30 pictures a second and your [[@microphones|microphone]] turns your voice into electrical signals. Software squeezes these into a much smaller bundle of data. The internet carries the bundle to the other person in small packets. Their device unpacks it, rebuilds the picture and plays your voice.
All this has to happen in well under half a second. If it takes longer, people start talking over each other, and the call begins to feel like a walkie-talkie.

Most frames are not full pictures. Usually only the changes are sent, such as your mouth moving or a hand waving, and a full picture is sent now and then. The wall behind you is hardly sent at all.

sec.t:
A camera picture is a grid of tiny coloured dots called [[@pixels|pixels]]. A normal HD frame has about 920,000 of them. Each [[pixel|pixel]] is stored as three numbers for red, green and blue.

Do the maths for 30 frames a second and raw HD video comes to roughly 650 megabits every second. That would choke a typical home internet line many times over. So video calls can never send raw video. They have to shrink it.

sec.h: The art of throwing things away
sec.t:
The shrinking is done by a codec, short for coder-decoder. It uses two big tricks. First, it drops detail your eyes are bad at noticing, like tiny shades of colour. Second, it sends only what changes from one frame to the next.

If you sit still in front of a plain wall, the wall barely needs sending at all. Your blinking eyes and moving lips get most of the data. That is why the picture turns blocky when you wave your arms or walk around. Suddenly everything is changing, and the codec can't keep up.

A typical HD call ends up using about 1–3 megabits a second, hundreds of times less than the raw video.

sec.t:
Your speaker plays the other person's voice, and your microphone could pick it straight back up. They would hear their own voice return a moment later, which is maddening. So apps run echo cancellation. Software knows exactly what sound it just played and subtracts it from what the microphone hears.

Since [[@sound-travel|sound travels]] at about 343 metres a second, even a small room creates echoes that the software has to tidy away.

sec.h: From World's Fair dream to every pocket
sec.t:
The US phone company AT&T showed off a Picturephone at the 1964 New York World's Fair. Visitors could chat with strangers in California, on a small black-and-white screen. It cost a fortune to use and flopped. Public booths opened in 1964, but three minutes between New York and Chicago cost about $27, a huge sum then.

Ordinary internet video calls took off in the 2000s with apps like Skype. Then came 2020. When schools and offices closed during the COVID-19 lockdowns, Zoom said its daily meeting participants jumped from about 10 million in December 2019 to about 300 million in April 2020. Children in India and the USA suddenly went to class through a screen. Their Wi-Fi carried them there on invisible [[@radio-waves|radio waves]].

text: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Maryland, escaped to freedom in 1849, and then risked her life to guide others out. She became the best-known "conductor" on the [[@usa-underground-railroad|Underground Railroad]], a secret network of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape to the North.

During the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]] she worked for the Union army as a nurse, a scout and a spy. Later she campaigned for women's right to vote and cared for poor and elderly people. She never learned to read, yet she planned journeys across hundreds of kilometres of enemy country and, by her own account, never lost a person she was guiding.

st.prompt: Tubman usually led her escapes in winter, and often started on a Saturday night. Why Saturday?

options.t: Newspapers couldn't print "runaway" notices until Monday

st.reveal: Notices offering rewards for runaways usually could not appear until the Monday papers. Leaving on Saturday gave her group a head start. Long winter nights also gave more hours of darkness.

sec.t:
She was born around 1822 and named Araminta Ross. Her family called her "Minty". As a small child she was hired out to other families, made to check muskrat traps in icy water and to look after babies through the night.

When she was a teenager, an overseer threw a heavy weight at another enslaved person, and it struck her head instead. She was badly hurt. For the rest of her life she had headaches and sudden sleeping spells.

In 1849, fearing she would be sold away from her family, she escaped. She travelled mostly at night, about 145 km, to Pennsylvania, where slavery was illegal. She took a new name, Harriet, after her mother, and her husband's surname, Tubman.

"I had crossed the line," she said later. "I was free; but there was no one to welcome me." So she went back.

When the Civil War began in 1861, during [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]]'s presidency, Tubman joined Union forces in South Carolina. She nursed soldiers and organised a network of scouts. In June 1863 she helped guide Union gunboats up the Combahee River. Enslaved people ran to the boats, and more than 700 were freed. She was one of the first women in US history to help lead an armed raid.

She was paid very little for her war service, and she spent years asking the government for the pension she was owed. After the war, [[@slavery-freedom|slavery ended]] across the country, the goal she had worked for since her escape.

Tubman settled in Auburn, New York. She spoke at meetings for [[@womens-vote|women's right to vote]], and opened a home for elderly Black people on her land. She died in 1913, aged around 90, and was buried with military honours.

Her home in Auburn and places in Maryland where she grew up are now national historical parks. In 2016 the US Treasury announced plans to put her portrait on the 20-dollar note, but in 2026 it said it was no longer working on the change.

text: Raja Ram Mohan Roy was a scholar and reformer from Bengal who lived from about 1772 to 1833. He is often called one of the makers of modern India. He campaigned against sati, the custom in some communities of a widow dying on her husband's funeral pyre. He argued for women's rights, modern education and a free press, and started a new religious movement, the Brahmo Samaj.
He did all this at a time when the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] ruled Bengal, and many of the debates he started went on long after his death.

st.reveal: Some groups in India had appealed to London to overturn the 1829 ban on sati. Roy went to argue for keeping it, and also to put the case of the Mughal emperor Akbar II, who gave him the title Raja. He never came home.

sec.t:
Ram Mohan Roy was born in the village of Radhanagar in Bengal, into a Brahmin family. As a young man he studied Persian and Arabic, the languages of government and learning under Mughal rule, and Sanskrit, the language of Hindu [[scripture|scripture]]. Later he learned English, and he is said to have studied Hebrew and Greek too.

Reading so widely made him ask questions. He found that the oldest Hindu texts, the Upanishads, spoke of one formless God. He began to argue that many later customs, including idol worship and some harsh rules for women, were not found in these texts at all.

Roy believed people needed information to think for themselves. In the early 1820s he started newspapers in Bengali and Persian. When the government brought in strict rules on printing in 1823, he protested publicly, in an early campaign for [[@free-speech|free speech]] in India.

He also wanted Indian students to learn science, mathematics and English alongside Indian languages. He supported new schools in Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], and argued that modern subjects would help India more than learning by rote.

In 1828, Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in Calcutta, later called the Brahmo Samaj. Its members met to worship one God without idols, using readings from the Upanishads and hymns. The movement attracted many thinkers, including members of the Tagore family. It played a big part in what is called the [[@bengali-renaissance|Bengal Renaissance]], a burst of new ideas in literature, science and society.

In 1830, the Mughal emperor Akbar II, by then a ruler in name only, gave Roy the title "Raja" and sent him to Britain to plead for a bigger pension. In England, Roy met politicians and writers and was widely admired.

In 1833 he fell ill while visiting Bristol and died there. He is buried at Arnos Vale Cemetery, under a tomb shaped like a chhatri. A statue of him stands in the centre of Bristol, and the city still holds events in his memory.

Many Indians remember Roy as a brave reformer. Some historians point out that he worked closely with British officials and that the reforms he pushed mainly reached educated, upper-caste families at first. Still, later reformers such as [[@ishwar-chandra|Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar]], who campaigned for widows to remarry, built on the path he opened.

text: English got its Latin words in waves, over about 1,500 years. Churchmen brought Latin to England in the early Middle Ages. Then, after 1066, French-speaking rulers brought thousands of French words, and French itself had grown out of Latin. Later still, during the [[@renaissance|Renaissance]], scholars borrowed Latin words directly for science, law and learning.

The result is that about 60% of the words in a large English dictionary come from Latin, either directly or through French. English is still a Germanic language at heart. Its grammar and its most common short words come from Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons. But its vocabulary is a mixture.

Oddly, the Romans themselves left very few words behind. They ruled Britain from about 43 CE to 410 CE, but the people there spoke Celtic languages. English only arrived after the Romans left, when Angles, Saxons and other Germanic peoples crossed the North Sea.

st.reveal: After the Normans conquered England in 1066, French-speaking lords ate the meat while English-speaking farmers raised the animals. So English kept its own words for the animals (pig, cow, sheep) and borrowed French words for the meat (pork, beef, mutton). Those French words came from Latin.
