sec.t:
In 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, crossed from France and won the Battle of Hastings. For about 300 years afterwards, the kings and nobles of England spoke French, while ordinary people spoke English.

This split still shows in English. Farmers kept English words for living animals: cow, pig, sheep. The lords who ate the meat used French words: beef (*boeuf*), pork (*porc*) and mutton (*mouton*). Words for law and power, such as court, judge, [[@jury|jury]], government and crown, also arrived from French.

Eventually English became the language of the court again, but it kept thousands of these borrowed words. Often English ended up with two words for nearly the same thing: a plain Old English one and a fancier French one, such as "begin" and "commence", or "help" and "aid".

{{story:ancient-rome}}

From the 1500s, scholars across Europe still wrote in Latin. When English writers needed words for new ideas, they often built them from Latin parts. That is how English got words such as "[[species|species]]", "formula", "[[atmosphere|atmosphere]]" and "spectacles".

Many roots repeat across dozens of words. *Scrib* means write, giving describe and scribble. *Dict* means say, giving dictionary and predict. *Port* means carry, giving transport and portable. Learn a few roots and you can often guess a word you have never seen.

Science still names living things in Latin. A tiger is *Panthera tigris*, and humans are *Homo sapiens*, "wise human".

Latin turns up in everyday English without people noticing. "a.m." and "p.m." stand for *ante meridiem* and *post meridiem*, before and after midday. "etc." is *et cetera*, "and the rest". "e.g." is *exempli gratia*, "for example". [[@roman-numerals|Roman numerals]] still mark clock faces, film sequels and the [[@super-bowl|Super Bowl]].

The USA has a Latin motto on its money and seal: *E pluribus unum*, "out of many, one". Latin is also the official language of the Holy See, which runs the Catholic Church from [[@vatican|Vatican City]].

In 1786, a British judge in Calcutta named William Jones gave a famous talk. He had been studying [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and noticed it looked strangely similar to Latin and Greek. Sanskrit *trayas* and Latin *tres* both mean three. *Nava* and *novus* both mean new.

Jones suggested that all three languages came from a common ancestor that no longer existed. He was right. Scholars now call this family Indo-European. It includes Hindi, Bengali, Persian, Latin, Greek, English, German and many more. So when you say "mother" in English and *mata* in Hindi, you are using two branches of the same very old word.

text: Young children are not simply smarter at languages. They learn differently. A baby's brain is busily tuning itself to the sounds of whatever language it hears most. Children soak up grammar through play and chatter, without worrying about mistakes.

Older learners have advantages too. They can use rules, reading and memory tricks, so teenagers and adults often make faster progress at first. But people who start a language young are far more likely to end up sounding like a native speaker, especially in their accent.
How strict the "best age" really is remains one of the liveliest arguments in the science of language.

st.prompt: Babies from English-speaking homes heard two different Hindi "t" sounds. What happened by about their first birthday?

options.t: Most could no longer tell the two sounds apart
They could tell them apart even better

st.reveal: At six to eight months, most babies heard the difference easily. By ten to twelve months, most had lost it, because English doesn't use that difference. Their brains had tuned in to the sounds that mattered around them.

sec.t:
In the early 1980s, the Canadian psychologist Janet Werker tested babies from English-speaking families on sounds from [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] and from a language of western Canada. Hindi has two different "t" sounds: one with the tongue curled back, as in *tamatar*, and one with the tongue against the teeth, as in *taal*. Most English-speaking adults hear them as the same.

At six to eight months old, the babies could hear the difference. By ten to twelve months, most had lost that ability. The American researcher Patricia Kuhl found something similar with Japanese babies and the English sounds "r" and "l". A baby's [[@brain-works|brain]] seems to become an expert in the sounds that matter around it, and stops paying attention to the rest.

In much of India, children grow up with two or three languages: one at home, one at school and one in the street or on the cricket field. A child in Bengaluru might speak Kannada with friends, Hindi with neighbours, Tamil with grandparents and English in class. Across [[@languages-india|India's many languages]], this is ordinary, not special.

Being bilingual does not confuse children, as some parents once feared. Children may mix two languages in one sentence, but that is a normal stage, and often a clever use of both. Deaf children who learn [[@sign-language|sign language]] from birth reach the same milestones as hearing children who learn to speak.

Adults can and do learn new languages, sometimes brilliantly. Joseph Conrad grew up speaking Polish and also learned French. He only began learning English in his twenties, yet he became one of the great novelists in the English language. His strong Polish accent stayed with him all his life.

That is the usual pattern. Grammar and vocabulary can be mastered at almost any age, with enough practice, but an accent is hard to change after childhood. Conrad wrote all his famous novels in English, his third language, accent and all.

text: William Shakespeare was an English playwright and poet who lived from 1564 to 1616. He wrote about 37 plays, including Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, Macbeth and A Midsummer Night's Dream, and 154 short poems called [[sonnet|sonnets]].

He is still famous for three main reasons. His stories are gripping, with murders, ghosts, [[@twins|twins]], [[@shipwrecks|shipwrecks]] and young lovers. His characters feel like real people with mixed-up feelings. And his language was so memorable that many of his phrases are still in everyday English, used by people who have never read a word of him.

st.reveal: Women were not allowed to act on the public stage in England in Shakespeare's day. Teenage boys, whose voices had not yet broken, played the female roles. Women began appearing on English stages only in the 1660s.

sec.h: A glover's son from a market town
sec.t:
Shakespeare grew up in Stratford-upon-Avon, a market town in central England. His father made gloves. At 18 he married Anne Hathaway, and they had three children. By the early 1590s he was in [[@london|London]], working as an actor and writer.

He became a partner in an acting company and helped build a playhouse called the Globe in 1599. It was round, open to the sky, and held up to about 3,000 people. Poorer people stood in the yard in front of the stage for a penny. In 1613 a cannon fired during a play set the thatched roof alight, and the Globe burned down. A careful copy, Shakespeare's Globe, opened near the old site in 1997.

sec.h: The book that saved his plays

sec.t:
Phrases like "wild-goose chase" and "break the ice" became popular through his plays, though some were already around before him. Many of his lines have become common sayings: "to be, or not to be" and "all the world's a stage".

He wrote in verse a lot of the time, using a [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] called iambic pentameter, which goes da-DUM five times in a line. Try saying "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks" and you can hear the beat. Kings and lovers often speak in verse, while servants and clowns often speak in plain prose. That was one way Shakespeare showed who a character was.

Shakespeare reached India with the British, and Indian theatre groups were performing him in English, Bengali, Marathi, Urdu and other languages by the 1800s. Over time he was adapted so fully that his stories now feel at home here.

The Hindi film Angoor (1982) is a comedy based on The Comedy of Errors, with two pairs of twins causing chaos. Director Vishal Bhardwaj set Macbeth among Mumbai gangsters in Maqbool (2003), Othello in rural Uttar Pradesh in Omkara (2006), and Hamlet in Kashmir in Haider (2014). In the United States, Romeo and Juliet became the musical West Side Story in 1957. Shakespeare's plots work because jealousy, ambition and first love have not changed since 1600, and [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] knows it.

text: Tongue twisters are hard because they pack similar sounds close together, in a confusing order. When you speak, your brain plans a few sounds ahead of your mouth. If two sounds are very alike, like "s" and "sh", the plans get mixed up and one sound slips into the wrong place.
Say "She sells seashells" slowly and it's easy. Speed up, and your brain has less time to keep the sounds apart. Out comes "she shells sea sells". The tongue just does what it's told.

st.prompt: Which pair of sounds is more likely to trip you up when you alternate them fast?

s and m, as in "six mice"

st.reveal: Sounds made in almost the same place in the mouth, in almost the same way, are easiest to mix up. S and sh differ only in a small shift of the tongue, so the brain's plans for them get tangled. S and m are made in very different ways, so they rarely clash.

sec.t:
Speaking is one of the most complicated things the [[@brain-works|brain]] does. To say a single word, it picks the word, lines up its sounds and sends signals to dozens of [[@muscles|muscles]] in your lips, tongue, jaw and throat, and to your [[@voice|voice box]]. All of this happens in a fraction of a second.

Your brain doesn't plan one sound at a time. It prepares a little ahead, like a queue of sounds waiting their turn. Most of the time, they come out in the right order. In a tongue twister, the queue is full of near-twins, and they jump places.

Linguists describe sounds by where and how they are made. "P" and "b" are both made with the lips. "S" and "sh" are both hissing sounds made with the tongue near the roof of the mouth, just a little apart. "T" and "k" are both quick stops, one at the front, one at the back.

Tongue twisters mix such pairs. "Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers" swaps p, k and t sounds. "The sixth sick sheikh's sixth sheep's sick", once named by Guinness [[@world-records|World Records]] as the hardest in English, packs s, sh, k and th into a tiny space.

In 2013, researchers at MIT tested volunteers with many twisters. "Pad kid poured curd pulled cod" was so hard that some people stopped altogether. It alternates p and k sounds at the start of words, and those two sounds are easy to confuse.

{{story:voice}}

Every language seems to have tongue twisters, and they use that language's tricky pairs. In [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], children try "kachcha [[@papad|papad]], pakka papad" fast, and the k and p sounds soon swap places. Another favourite is "Chandu ke chacha ne Chandu ki chachi ko chandi ke chammach se chatni chatai", a crowd of ch sounds.

Some languages have sounds that English lacks, so their twisters use different traps. Twisters in tonal languages like Mandarin play with words that differ only by pitch.

Tongue twisters are a kind of planned accident. Linguists study ordinary slips too, because mistakes show how speech is organised. When someone says "a blushing crow" instead of "a crushing blow", the swapped sounds reveal that the brain planned both words before speaking either.

These swaps are called spoonerisms, after William Archibald Spooner, an Oxford professor in the late 1800s who was said to make them often. Many of the famous ones were probably invented by his students.

Actors, singers, radio presenters and news readers use tongue twisters as warm-ups. Saying them slowly and clearly trains the muscles and the brain to keep sounds crisp. [[@theatre|Theatre]] schools have used them for generations.

Speech therapists sometimes use twisters to help people practise particular sounds. Writers love them too. Many of [[@dr-seuss|Dr. Seuss's]] books, such as Fox in Socks, are full of them. In the end, a tongue twister is a little game you play with your own brain, and the brain loses on purpose.

text: Maize, also called corn, was first farmed in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Its wild ancestor is a grass called teosinte, which has tiny ears with just a few hard seeds. Over thousands of years, farmers kept planting seeds from the plants they liked best: bigger ears, softer kernels, more rows. Slowly, teosinte became maize.

For most of history, maize grew only in the Americas. After 1492, European sailors carried it across the oceans. It spread fast, because it grows quickly, gives a big harvest from a small field and copes with many [[climate|climates]].
Today it is grown on every continent except Antarctica, and it is the world's biggest grain crop by weight.

sec.t:
Teosinte looks so different from maize that scientists argued for decades about whether they were related. [[dna|DNA]] studies settled it. Most experts now think maize came from teosinte growing in the Balsas River valley of [[@mexico|Mexico]].

The change was so complete that maize can no longer survive alone. Its seeds are wrapped tightly in husks and stuck to the cob, so they can't scatter. Without farmers to peel and plant them, maize would die out in a few years.

People in the Americas bred thousands of local kinds: red, blue, black, speckled, popping and sweet. The Maya creation story tells that the gods made the first humans out of maize dough.

{{story:farming-began}}

Eaten plain, maize is missing a B [[vitamin|vitamin]] called niacin in a form the body can easily use. Farmers in Mexico and Central America solved this long ago. They soaked and cooked dried kernels with lime or wood ash. This process, called [[nixtamalisation|nixtamalisation]], freed the niacin and made the dough easier to shape, which is why tortillas hold together.

When maize spread to Europe and parts of Africa, people often skipped this step. Where families ate little else, a disease called pellagra, which causes skin rashes and tiredness, became common. It took until the early 1900s to work out why.

[[@columbus|Columbus]] took maize back to Spain in 1493. Within a few decades it was growing in Italy, Turkey and Africa. Portuguese traders carried it along their sea routes, and it probably reached India in the 1500s.

It found a home here. In Punjab, winter means [[@punjabi-food|makki di roti]] with sarson ka saag. In the [[monsoon|monsoon]], street sellers roast bhutta over coals, rubbing them with lime and chilli salt. In the hills of Himachal and the north-east, maize is an everyday staple.

Today the world harvests well over a billion tonnes of maize a year. The USA grows the most, mainly across the Midwest "Corn Belt", followed by China. American farmers measure their harvest in bushels, and a big year's crop runs to well over 10 billion of them. India is among the top ten growers.

Most of it isn't eaten as corn on the cob. Large amounts feed [[@chickens|chickens]], pigs and cattle. In the USA, a big share is turned into ethanol, a fuel mixed into petrol. Maize also becomes corn [[starch|starch]], corn syrup and oil, used in thousands of foods, from ketchup to biscuits.

Some kinds of maize do something special. [[@popcorn|Popcorn]] kernels have a hard, waterproof shell. When heated, the water inside turns to steam and the kernel bursts, turning itself inside out.

People in the Americas were popping corn thousands of years ago. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] in Peru have found popped kernels more than 6,000 years old. The cinema snack in your hand comes from one of the oldest crops on the planet.

text: Junk food gives you lots of energy, usually from sugar, refined flour, oil and salt. But it has very little of what your body needs to grow and stay well, such as fibre, [[protein|protein]], [[@vitamins|vitamins]] and minerals.

[[@accident-potato-chips|Chips]], sweet [[@soft-drinks|fizzy drinks]], packaged cakes, [[@maggi-noodles|instant noodles]] and many fried snacks fit this description. They are made to taste great, last a long time on a shelf and be quick to eat. None of that is wicked. The trouble is that it is very easy to eat a lot of them, and if they crowd out other foods, your body misses out.

sec.h: Built to be hard to stop
sec.t:
Food companies employ scientists to find the right mix of sweet, salty and fatty that makes people want more. The journalist Michael Moss wrote about this in his book Salt Sugar Fat. Food scientists sometimes talk about the "bliss point", the amount of sugar that makes a product most pleasing.

Many snacks also melt quickly or crunch loudly, which makes them feel light even when they carry lots of [[calorie|calories]]. That is part of [[@taste-why|why we like]] some foods so much more than others.

In about 2009, Brazilian scientist Carlos Monteiro and his team suggested sorting foods by how much they are processed. "Ultra-processed" foods are made mostly from factory ingredients, like syrups, [[starch|starches]] and flavourings, rather than whole foods.

In 2019 a team at the US National Institutes of Health tested this. Twenty adults lived in a lab for four weeks. When given ultra-processed meals, they ate about 500 more calories a day than when given meals made from whole foods, even though they could eat as much as they liked of both.

Not all fried or tasty food is junk. A [[@samosa|samosa]], a plate of pakoras or a slice of homemade cake is fine as an occasional treat. A samosa also has potatoes and peas inside it.

What matters most is the overall pattern. Dal, rice, vegetables, fruit, curd and nuts most days leave plenty of room for treats. The problem comes when packaged snacks and sweet drinks become the everyday food instead.

Some countries now put bold warnings on unhealthy foods. In 2016 Chile began requiring black stop-sign [[@food-labels|labels]] on packets high in sugar, salt, fat or calories, and limited cartoon characters in adverts for them. Mexico and others followed. India and the United States have been debating front-of-pack labels for years.

Labels help, but so does reading the small print. Packets often list a "serving" that is much smaller than what people really eat. A bag of chips might say it holds three servings, even though most people finish it in one go. Numbers can be true and still give the wrong idea, a trick explained in [[@statistics-lies|how statistics can mislead]].

Advertising matters too. Snacks are often sold with cartoon characters, free toys and famous cricketers or footballers. That is why some countries now limit junk food adverts during children's television shows.
